newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals - LME copper slump cuts Japan premiums.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - LME copper slump cuts Japan premiums.

text.p: Copper's slump on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Tuesday has depressed the metal's premium in Japan amid talk of ample deliveries from China and South Korea, traders said on Wednesday.
"Three-month fell sharply overnight. Such a large decline leads to lower (Japanese) premiums," said a trader at one of Japan's leading trading companies.
"Though these price levels should trigger some buying, we hear many have quite a lot of stocks," he added.
Traders said Japanese copper premiums over the LME prices were quoted at $50-60 per tonne, down from $60-70 a week ago.
In addition to weak domestic demand, talk of copper deliveries of up to 80,000 tonnes from China and South Korea to a Singapore warehouse were weighing on the market, they said.
Yet some noted the fall in copper through a major support at $2,300 on Tuesday may help a South Korean firm rumoured to hold huge short positions.

Late last month, South Korea's largest copper producer LG Metals Corp said it had sold about 10,000 tonnes of copper to Germany's Metallgesellschaft AG, a move some traders said was aimed at covering its short positions on the LME.
Meanwhile, some Japanese traders were pinning hopes that the continuing heatwave would boost demand for copper through higher sales of air conditioners.
Aluminium traders were also watching whether the hot weather would propel higher demand for air conditioners and beverage cans.
Aluminium's premium remained high at $95-100 per tonne for deliveries in the current quarter, though they were $80-85 for the fourth quarter of 1996.
"Should demand for beverage cans show strong growth, premiums may stay at current high levels," said one trader.
"They say one sunny day means 500 tonnes of more of aluminium demand."

In the physical zinc market, premiums for Chinese special high grade (SHG) dropped to $30-40 per tonne from $40-50 a week ago -- despite strong Japanese demand as high LME prices encouraged the Chinese to export, traders said.
"There are quite a lot of sellers, mostly from China," said one trader, adding that he was watching the outcome of ongoing talks between China and Swiss trader Glencore AG.

Earlier this week, Chinese industry sources said the country's state metals units and Glencore were in talks since Sunday to resolve a dispute that arose over the quality of Chinese metal and could threaten links between the two.

The trader also said he was waiting for the Swiss trader to make clear to whom it planned to sell zinc produced by Spain's Austriana de Zinc S.A, one of the world's largest smelters with an annual production of about 300,000 tonnes.
Glencore said on Tuesday that it had proposed to boost its stake in Austriana to 40 percent from current 25 percent.

A European house trader, citing a report in a Chinese local newspaper that heavy rainfall had caused severe floods in the south China coastal province of Guangdong, said Chinese exports could decrease temporarily due to transportation problems.
"If Chinese exports drop, the metal's price on the LME would rise further," he said.

Traders said the latest rally in zinc was making zinc production look attractive to many producers, including Anvil Range Mining Corp in Canada which said on Monday it agreed in principle to a loan to fund a stripping programme at its Grum ore deposit in Faro, Yukon.

"If it (Anvil) really resumes zinc ore production, it would have quite an impact on the market," said one trader. "At the moment smelters expect its first product towards the turn of the year, while mines say Anvil won't reopen Faro mine."
-- Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-6179
